title: Đọc Vị Bất Kỳ Ai (You Can Read Anyone)
author: T.S. David J. Lieberman
summary:
**Important note before this summary: the catalog title you provided combines two different, unrelated books.** "Kế Toán Vỉa Hè" is the Vietnamese title of "The Accounting Game: Basic Accounting Fresh from the Lemonade Stand" by Darrell Mullis and Judith Orloff — a basic-accounting primer that has nothing to do with David J. Lieberman. "Đọc Vị Bất Kỳ Ai" is the Vietnamese title of David J. Lieberman's "You Can Read Anyone," which does match the author you listed. Since your slug and author point clearly to Lieberman, this entry covers "Đọc Vị Bất Kỳ Ai / You Can Read Anyone" only. If you also own "Kế Toán Vỉa Hè" as a separate physical book, it should get its own catalog entry in a future batch — flagging this now so the mix-up doesn't get carried forward.

David J. Lieberman's You Can Read Anyone is built around a practical claim: that with the right set of targeted questions and observational cues, an ordinary person — not just a trained interrogator or psychologist — can accurately read what someone else is thinking or feeling in a real, specific situation, without resorting to guesswork, generic body-language tips, or manipulative pressure tactics. Lieberman frames his approach as more systematic than typical "read their body language" advice, built instead around what he calls the S.N.A.P. approach: a structured way of analyzing personality and intent that draws on psychological research rather than pop-culture gesture-reading.

The book is organized around a series of concrete, everyday situations rather than abstract theory: is this person being honest with me, is a business partner trustworthy, is a new hire going to work well under pressure, is a friend or partner actually upset even though they're saying they're fine. For each scenario, Lieberman provides specific diagnostic questions and behavioral cues to look for, explaining the psychological reasoning behind why a given answer or reaction pattern reveals what it does.

A second half of the book moves beyond surface-level reading into understanding how people actually make decisions — what Lieberman describes as getting past reading isolated thoughts and feelings toward understanding someone's underlying decision-making process well enough to anticipate how they'll act in a new situation, not just how they feel about the current one. This is presented as a more advanced, but still learnable, extension of the book's core diagnostic approach.

Throughout, Lieberman is careful to frame the book's techniques as tools for accurate understanding and self-protection — catching dishonesty, avoiding being taken advantage of, communicating more effectively — rather than as manipulation tools, and repeatedly grounds his claims in behavioral and psychological research rather than presenting them as pure intuition or folk wisdom.

sections.title: Part One: Seven Basic Questions
sections.summary:
This opening part introduces a core set of diagnostic questions Lieberman argues can be used across a wide range of everyday situations to quickly assess what someone is really thinking or feeling, moving past their stated position to their underlying state.
It explains the psychological reasoning behind why these particular questions work — often because they're difficult to answer convincingly while lying or concealing true feelings, in ways a direct "are you being honest with me?" question is not.
It sets up the more detailed, scenario-specific chapters that build on this basic toolkit.
keyLessons: Indirect diagnostic questions often reveal more than direct confrontational ones.
The same small set of core questions can be adapted across many different everyday situations.
Reading people accurately is presented as a learnable skill built on specific technique, not raw intuition.

sections.title: Part Two: Blueprints for the Mind — Understanding Decision-Making
sections.summary:
This part moves beyond reading a single thought or feeling in the moment toward understanding a person's broader decision-making patterns, so the reader can better anticipate how someone is likely to act in future, not-yet-encountered situations.
It covers how to identify recurring patterns in how someone weighs risk, handles pressure, or resolves competing priorities, using past behavior as a guide to likely future behavior.
It closes by tying this deeper pattern-reading back to the book's practical goal: better decisions in hiring, partnerships, and relationships based on genuine understanding rather than surface impressions.
keyLessons: Understanding someone's decision-making pattern is more predictive than reading a single momentary reaction.
Past behavior under specific conditions (pressure, risk, competing priorities) is a strong guide to likely future behavior.
The goal of deeper reading is better real-world decisions, not just accurate labeling of someone's current mood.
Use indirect, specific diagnostic questions rather than direct confrontational ones to assess honesty.
Treat reading people as a learnable, systematic skill rather than pure intuition or generic body-language tips.
Match your diagnostic approach to the specific real situation (hiring, honesty-checking, gauging a partner's true feelings) rather than using one generic method.
Look at patterns in past behavior under pressure to anticipate likely future decisions.
Use these skills primarily for accurate understanding and self-protection, not manipulation.
Recognize that stated feelings ("I'm fine") often diverge from underlying emotional state, and specific questions can surface that gap.
Ground your read on someone in multiple consistent cues, not a single isolated signal.
Apply the same underlying diagnostic principles across personal, professional, and transactional relationships.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The S.N.A.P. Approach
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Lieberman's structured framework for analyzing personality and intent in a systematic, research-grounded way, positioned in the book as a more rigorous alternative to generic body-language or gesture-based "reading people" advice.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Seven Basic Questions
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A core set of specific, situation-adaptable diagnostic questions the book presents as a starting toolkit for quickly assessing what someone is really thinking or feeling in a given interaction.

actionSteps: The next time you suspect someone isn't being fully honest with you, try one of the book's indirect diagnostic questions instead of asking directly whether they're lying.
Before a significant conversation (a negotiation, a hiring decision, a difficult personal talk), write down what you already know about that person's past behavior under similar pressure.
Practice noticing when someone's stated feeling ("I'm fine") seems inconsistent with other cues, and ask one specific follow-up question rather than accepting the statement at face value.
Pick one important relationship (business or personal) and try to identify a recurring pattern in how that person makes decisions under competing priorities.
reflectionQuestions: Where in your life have you relied on surface impressions of someone rather than a more systematic read of their actual patterns?
Have you ever used "reading people" techniques in a way that tipped from understanding into manipulation — and how would you know the difference?
Whose future behavior would it be most useful for you to be able to anticipate more accurately right now?

points: Lieberman's books are written for a broad popular audience and, while they reference psychological research, they generally don't provide citations rigorous enough for a reader to independently verify specific claims against the underlying studies.

"Reading people" claims of this kind — accurately inferring internal states from behavioral cues — are an area where academic psychology (particularly deception-detection research) has found much weaker and less reliable effects than popular books in this genre often suggest, a body of caution this book doesn't heavily engage with.

Techniques framed as being for "self-protection" and "understanding" can, in practice, be used for manipulation or control, and the line between reading someone accurately and pressuring them isn't always as clean in real interactions as the book's framing implies.

The promotional claims about use by organizations like the FBI or military (as circulated in marketing material) are difficult to independently verify and should be treated skeptically rather than as evidence of the book's scientific rigor.
criticalTake.contextNote: Popular deception-detection and "reading people" claims broadly have faced increasing scrutiny from psychological researchers in the years since this genre of book became popular, which is useful context for readers applying its techniques with real confidence in high-stakes situations.

whoThisIsFor: Readers wanting a structured, question-based approach to assessing honesty and understanding others in everyday personal and professional situations.
whenToReadThis: Most useful before a specific high-stakes interaction (a hire, a negotiation, a trust decision) rather than as passive general reading.

authorBio.name: David J. Lieberman
authorBio.bio:
David J. Lieberman is an American psychotherapist and author who has written a series of popular psychology books focused on interpersonal understanding, persuasion, and behavior change, several of which have been translated into many languages, including Vietnamese, and have been marketed toward business, law-enforcement, and general readers alike.

His work generally packages psychological concepts into structured, question-based or step-based frameworks intended to be immediately usable by a lay reader without clinical training.

sourceNotes:
Synthesis is based on general knowledge of David J. Lieberman's well-known "You Can Read Anyone" and its S.N.A.P.-based, question-driven approach, cross-checked against Vietnamese-language search results describing this specific translated edition's two-part structure ("Bảy câu hỏi cơ bản" / Seven Basic Questions, and a second part on understanding decision-making). I want to flag clearly, as noted at the top of the Summary, that your original catalog entry combined two unrelated books under one title/slug — this entry covers only the Lieberman book matching the given author; "Kế Toán Vỉa Hè" (The Accounting Game, by Mullis & Orloff) is a separate, unrelated title that should get its own entry if you want it included. Quotes section is intentionally thin and flagged rather than padded, since verified exact-wording passages could not be confidently located.
